title: Improving Topic Modeling by Distilling Soft Labels from Language Models
topic: General Machine Learning->Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Learning
claim: Reconstruction targets built from word counts only reach words present in the text; soft labels from a language model also capture unseen themes.
layout: 2 panels under a text box, side-by-side mirrored bar charts, gray versus green
description: A rounded text box at the top holds a 20Newsgroups post about hockey, the Ottawa Sun, the Nordiques and the Flyers. Some words are bolded and underlined, such as going, million, paid, include, draft, real, having and good. Below it are two mirrored horizontal bar charts that share a layout. The left chart, labeled BoW, has gray bars for words that appear in the document: going, million, real, paid, good and others. These are generic words with low mass. The right chart, labeled DSL, has green bars for words including sports, hockey, public, report, media and news. Its x-axis runs from 0.15 down to 0. The eye goes first to the long green sports bar. The contrast shows that DSL gives mass to thematic words that never appear in the text.
caption: Comparison of BoW target (left) versus DSL target (right) for a document in the 20Newsgroups dataset. BoW can only assign mass to words that appear in the document ({bolded}), while the DSL target captures the underlying themes of the sports commentary even when the words don't explicitly appear in the document (e.g., "sports", "hockey").
abstract: Traditional neural topic models are typically optimized by reconstructing the document's Bag-of-Words (BoW) representations, overlooking contextual information and struggling with data sparsity. In this work, we introduce a novel topic model training framework by Distilling Soft Labels (DSL) from Language Models (LMs). To construct the contextually enriched reconstruction signals, we project the next token probabilities, conditioned on a specialized prompt, onto a pre-defined vocabulary, and train the topic models to reconstruct the soft labels using the LM hidden states. This produces higher-quality topics that are more closely aligned with the underlying thematic structure of the corpus. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSL achieves substantial improvements in topic coherence and assignment accuracy over existing baselines. Additionally, we also introduce a retrieval-based metric, which shows that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in identifying semantically similar documents, highlighting its effectiveness for retrieval-oriented applications.
